"That's the exact right question to ask, because one day there will be overcapacity and the party's over. Not there yet. You can measure that by spot rental prices for GPUs. "So fair enough, let's look at it this way. There's 10,000 data centers out there, most of which are CPU based. The vast majority of them need to be GPU based. We're about 1,000 to 1,400 of the way into that process. Don't need CPUs where we're going. We need GPUs."

"If you look at the value from these agents, you are starting to see glimmers of labor displacement. We're still in the labor productivity part of the curve, by the way, which means that people are far more productive. It's creating more work for everybody."

"You see glimmers of labor displacement, like I mentioned with agentic wealth management. You're starting to see agents that can do discovery better than an adviser, interactive discovery. How much are you willing to pay for that? A lot. Because it allows you to focus your people on higher value added activities and upskilling."

"Why wouldn't you spend $5,000 on an agent that can do SDR work, sales development representative work, that would otherwise cost $60,000, $80,000 or $120,000? Austin on why inflation isn't hitting everyone equally: higher rates turned government debt into a payout for people who already own assets

"Think about sort of money at a very macro level. Let's zoom out for a moment on where the particular flows are going. At the government level, you can simplify it to 2 things, which is money that the government is spending and money that the government is taking in."

"Because all of the ways government takes money in, which is through various programs and mostly through taxes, is one side of the ledger. The other side of the ledger is all of the ways in which government spends money, right? Social benefits programs, defense, like, interest service on debt."

"It's just a net inflow and a net outflow, and the differential of those is the amount of increase or reduction in the money supply due to the actions of the government. If we spend $8 trillion and take in $5 trillion, that's a plus $3 trillion, right?"

"All that money does have to come out somewhere. If you look at the variable that's been increasing the fastest as rates have gone up, that's payments on government debt, right? Who holds government debt, it is largely the investing class."

"Why is inflation not hitting everywhere equally, what is going on with the debasement trade? Why do assets continue to run? It's the biggest, positive plus, and where the money is coming into the hands of people who already have brokerage accounts or who are institutional investors, because they're the ones who own the T-bills, right?"

"Your average, 25 year old who just got a job and only has been out there for 3 years and doesn't have savings, probably a negative net worth with student debt, right, does not have a giant pile of T-bills. But your 65 year old mother does."

THORChain cofounder Chad Barraford admits 4 operators could halt THORChain, but argues Bitcoin and Ethereum can be stopped by even fewer

Laura: You said, quote, 'A chain may claim to have hundreds of validators, but that number means very little if most of them are operated by the same entities, hosted in the same data centers, or selected through a closed process.'"

"But THORChain itself has less than hundreds. And as we mentioned earlier, there are just 4 operator addresses that control 39 nodes. So do you think that THORChain passes your own litmus test?"

Chad: "Yeah. I think when it comes to evaluating how decentralized a protocol is, number of validators, not a good way to do it. And I'm not citing THORChain as decentralized because there's 115-ish validators. I'm saying it's decentralized because it has 50, 60, whatever the number is, individual operators across the world, which is better than Bitcoin, right?"

"Bitcoin's got 3, like, mining pools together would be 51% of the computing. Same thing for Ethereum. They've got, like, what, 3 or 4 operators with the major validators of Ethereum, and you would have the same situation. And most of those are, by the way, corporate entities, like Coinbase and Binance and these kinds of things."

"THORChain is more decentralized than Bitcoin and Ethereum, by the definition that you're granting to me in this moment."

"If you look at, like, halting, meaning the ability to stop the production of blocks, you would need 1/3 plus 1. It's something different if you categorize it as, like, a 2/3 majority to control the blockchain rather than stopping it."

"Even if you take the lesser of the two and you do, like, 1/3 plus 1, you can get 4 operators to, you know, stop the entire protocol. I don't know why they would do that, because you'd be burning your own RUNE to zero, which is not really in their financial interest to do so. But theoretically, on paper, they could do that."

"There's only, like, 3 entities you would need for Bitcoin, and, like, 1 or 2, or whatever the number is, for Ethereum. That's just, like, that is the world, right?"
